title: De Gratia Christi Et De Peccato Originali Contra Pelagium Et Coelestinum
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040.stoa046.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: plenitudo enim legis caritas, caritas autem dei non per legem diffusa est in cordibus nostris, sed per spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis. proinde per legem gratia demonstratur. ut lex per gratiam compleatur. quid enim iuuat Pelagium, quia diuersis uerbis eandem rem dicit, ut non intellegatur in lege atque doctrina gratiam constituere, qua possibilitatem naturae asserit adiuuari? quantum autem existimo, ideo ueretur intellegi, quia damnauit eos, qui dicunt gratiam dei et adiutorium non ad singulos actus dari, sed in libero arbitrio esse uel in lege atque doctrina, et tamen latere se putat, cum aliis atque aliis locutionibus uersat significationem legis atque doctrinae.
passages.english: For love is the fulfilment of the law, but the love of God has been poured into our hearts not through the law but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Accordingly, grace is shown through the law, so that the law may be fulfilled through grace. For what does it help Pelagius that he says the same thing in different words, so that he may not be understood to place grace in the law and teaching, [grace] by which he asserts that the possibility of nature is assisted? But, as far as I judge, he fears being understood for this reason: because he condemned those who say that the grace and help of God is not given for individual acts, but lies in free choice or in the law and teaching; and yet he thinks he escapes notice when he turns over the meaning of "law and teaching" in one phrase after another.

passages.original: quorum autem sit fides et quibus persuadetur, ut ad eum ueniant, satis ipse demonstrauit, ubi ait: nemo uenit ad me, nisi pater qui misit me traxerit eum, et paulo post, cum de non credentibus loqueretur, dixi, inquit, uobis, quia nemo potest uenire ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum a patre meo. hanc debet Pelagius gratiam confiteri, si uult non solum uocari, uerum etiam esse christianus.
passages.english: But whose the faith is, and who are persuaded to come to him, he himself showed clearly enough when he said: "No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him"; and a little later, when he was speaking about those who did not believe, he says: "I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted him by my Father." This grace Pelagius ought to confess, if he wishes not only to be called a Christian but actually to be one.

passages.original: si enim solum posse nostrum hac gratia iuuaretur, ita diceret dominus: omnis, qui audiuit a patre et didicit, potest uenire ad me; non autem ita dixit, sed omnis, qui audiuit, inquit, a patre et didicit, uenit ad me. uenire posse in natura ponit Pelagius uel etiam, ut modo dicere coepit, in gratia, qualemlibet eam sentiat, <qua ipsa\', ut dicit, \'possibilitas adiuuatur\'; uenire autem iam in uoluntate et opere est. non est autem consequens, ut qui potest uenire, etiam ueniat, nisi id uoluerit atque fecerit.
passages.english: For if only our ability were helped by this grace, the Lord would have said thus: "Everyone who has heard from the Father and has learned is able to come to me"; but he did not say this; rather he says, "Everyone who has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me." Pelagius places the ability to come in nature, or even, as he has lately begun to say, in grace, however he understands it, "by which", as he says, "the possibility itself is helped"; but coming is already a matter of will and deed. And it does not follow that one who is able to come also comes, unless he has willed it and done it.
passages.notes: The quotation marks in this passage are garbled in the scanned text; the sense is clear.

passages.original: non solum enim deus posse nostrum donauit atque adiuuat, sed etiam uelle et operari operatur in nobis, non quia nos non uolumus aut nos non agimus, sed quia sine ipsius adiutorio nec uolumus aliquid boni nec agimus. quomodo enim dicitur: \'quod possumus bene agere, dei est, quod autem agimus, nostrum est\\ cum dicat apostolus orare se ad deum pro eis, ad quos scribebat, ne quid mali faciant et ut quod bonum est faciant? non enim ait: oramus, ut possitis nihil facere mali, sed ne quid faciatis mali, nec: ut possitis bonum facere, sed: ut bonum faciatis, quoniam de quibus scriptum est: quotquot enim spiritu dei aguntur, hi filii sunt dei, profecto ut agant quod bonum est, ab illo aguntur qui bonus est. quomodo dicit Pelagius: \'quod bene loqui possumus, dei est, quod bene loquimur, nostrum est\\ cum dicat dominus: spiritus patris uestri est qui loquitur in uobis? neque enim ait: non uos estis, qui dedistis uobis posse bene loqui, sed ait: non uos estis qui loquimini, nec ait: spiritus patris uestri est, qui uobis dat uel dedit posse bene loqui, sed ait: qui loquitur in uobis, non significans possibilitatis profectum, sed exprimens cooperationis effectum.
passages.english: For God has not only given and helps our ability, but also works in us the willing and the working; not because we do not will or we do not act, but because without his help we neither will anything good nor do it. For how is it said, "That we are able to do good is God's, but that we do it is ours," when the apostle says that he prays to God for those to whom he was writing, that they may do nothing evil and that they may do what is good? For he does not say, "We pray that you may be able to do nothing evil," but "that you may do nothing evil"; nor "that you may be able to do good," but "that you may do good"; since of those of whom it is written, "For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God," it is certain that, in order that they may do what is good, they are led by him who is good. How does Pelagius say, "That we are able to speak well is God's, but that we speak well is ours," when the Lord says, "It is the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you"? For he does not say, "It is not you who gave yourselves the ability to speak well," but he says, "It is not you who speak"; nor does he say, "It is the Spirit of your Father who gives or has given you the ability to speak well," but he says, "who speaks in you," not signifying an advance in possibility but expressing the effect of cooperation.

passages.original: Sed ab his litteris Pelagius ad fidei suae librum uult transire lectorem, cuius uobis commemorationem fecit, in quo ea de quibus non interrogabatur multa disseruit. sed nos de quibus cum illis agimus, ipsa uideamus. cum enim ab unitate trinitatis usque ad resurrectionem carnis, quod ab illo nemo quaerebat, disputationem quantam uoluit terminasset, \'et baptisma\', inquit, unum tenemus, quod isdem sacramenti uerbis in infantibus quibus etiam in maioribus dicimus esse celebrandum\'.
passages.english: But from this letter Pelagius wants to send the reader over to the book of his faith, of which he made mention to you, in which he discussed at length many things about which he was not being questioned. But let us look at the very matters about which we are dealing with them. For when he had brought to a close, at whatever length he wished, a discussion running from the unity of the Trinity up to the resurrection of the flesh, which no one was asking of him, he says: "And we hold one baptism, which we say must be celebrated with the same words of the sacrament for infants as also for older people."

passages.original: \'Beatus\', inquit, \'Ambrosius episcopus, in cuius praecipue libris Romana elucet fides, qui scriptorum inter Latinos flos quidam speciosus enituit, cuius fidem et purissimum in scripturis sensum ne inimicus quidem ausus est reprehendere\'.
passages.english: "The blessed bishop Ambrose," he says, "in whose books above all the Roman faith shines out, who blossomed forth as a kind of beautiful flower among the Latin writers, whose faith and whose most pure understanding of the scriptures not even an enemy has dared to criticise."
passages.notes: The speaker quoted is Pelagius (made clear in the following context).

passages.original: Audiat ergo illum uenerabilem antistitem dicentem et docentem in secundo libro expositionis euangelii secundum Lucam cooperari dominum etiam uoluntatibus nostris. \'uides utique\', inquit, \'quia ubique domini uirtus studiis cooperatur humanis, ut nemo possit aedificare sine domino, nemo custodire sine domino, nemo quicquam incipere sine domino. et ideo iuxta apostolum siue manducatis siue bibitis, omnia in dei gloriam facite\'. uidetis quemadmodum sanctus Ambrosius etiam illud quod solent homines dicere \'nos incipimus et deus perficit\' his uerbis abstulit dicens neminem quicquam uel incipere sine deo. item in sexto libro eiusdem operis, cum de duobus illis unius feneratoris debitoribus ageret, \'secundum homines\', inquit, \'plus fortasse offendit, qui plus debuerat;
passages.english: Let him hear, then, that venerable bishop saying and teaching, in the second book of his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, that the Lord cooperates even with our wills. "You see, surely," he says, "that everywhere the power of the Lord cooperates with human efforts, so that no one can build without the Lord, no one keep watch without the Lord, no one begin anything without the Lord. And therefore, according to the apostle, whether you eat or drink, do all things to the glory of God." You see how holy Ambrose, with these words, has done away even with what people commonly say, "We begin and God completes," by saying that no one even begins anything without God. Likewise in the sixth book of the same work, when he was dealing with those two debtors of a single moneylender, he says: "By human reckoning, perhaps the one who had owed more gave greater offence;

passages.original: Ipsam denique paenitentiam, quam procul dubio uoluntas agit, domini misericordia et adiutorio fieri ut agatur, in nono eiusdem operis libro beatus dicit Ambrosius ita loquens: \'bonae lacrimae, quae culpam lauant. denique quos Iesus respicit, plorant. negauit primo Petrus et non fleuit, quia non respexerat dominus; negauit secundo, non fleuit, quia adhuc non respexerat dominus; negauit et tertio, respexit Iesus, et ille amarissime fleuit\'. legant isti euangelium et uideant dominum Iesum tunc intus fuisse, cum a sacerdotum principibus audiretur, apostolum uero Petrum foris et deorsum in atrio cum seruis ad focum nunc sedentem, nunc stantem, sicut ueracissima et concordissima euangelistarum narratione monstratur.
passages.english: Finally, blessed Ambrose says in the ninth book of the same work that repentance itself, which the will without doubt performs, comes to be performed by the mercy and help of the Lord, speaking thus: "Good are the tears that wash away guilt. Indeed, those on whom Jesus looks weep. Peter denied the first time and did not weep, because the Lord had not looked [at him]; he denied a second time, [and] did not weep, because the Lord had still not looked [at him]; he denied a third time too, Jesus looked [at him], and he wept most bitterly." Let these people read the Gospel and see that the Lord Jesus was inside at that time, when he was being heard by the chief priests, while the apostle Peter was outside and below in the courtyard with the servants by the fire, now sitting, now standing, as is shown by the most truthful and most harmonious narrative of the evangelists.

passages.original: Item in eodem libro idem sanctus Ambrosius \'nam si Petrus\', inquit, \'lapsus est, qui dixit: et si alii scandalizati fuerint, ego non scandalizabor, quis alius iure de se praesumat? denique Dauid quia dixerat: ego dixi in mea abundantia: non mouebor in aeternum, suam sibi iactantiam obfuisse profitetur dicens: auertisti faciem tuam et factus sum conturbatus\'. audiat iste tantum uirum docentem, imitetur credentem, cuius doctrinam fidemque laudauit; audiat humiliter imitetur fideliter; non de se pertinaciter praesumat, ne pereat. quid in eo pelago uult mergi Pelagius, unde per petram liberatus est Petrus? \'
passages.english: Likewise in the same book the same holy Ambrose says: "For if Peter fell, who said, 'Even if others are made to stumble, I will not be made to stumble,' who else could rightly presume about himself? Finally David, because he had said, 'I said in my abundance: I shall never be moved,' confesses that his boasting harmed him, saying: 'You turned away your face, and I was troubled.'" Let this man listen to so great a man teaching, let him imitate the one believing, whose teaching and faith he has praised; let him listen humbly, imitate faithfully; let him not stubbornly presume about himself, lest he perish. Why does Pelagius want to be drowned in that sea (pelagus) from which Peter was freed through the rock (petra)?
passages.notes: Wordplay in the Latin: pelago/Pelagius and petram/Petrus. A stray quotation mark ends the text.

passages.original: uidete, si non illud est propheticum: miserebor, cuius misertus ero, et misericordiam praestabo, cui misericors fuero, et illud apostolicum: igitur non uolentis neque currentis, sed miserentis est dei, qui, ut dicit etiam nostrorum temporum homo eius, \'quem dignatur uocat et quem uult religiosum facit\'. numquid aliquis dicere audebit nondum esse religiosum, (qui currit ad dominum et ab eo se regi cupit et uoluntatem suam ex eius uoluntate suspendit et qui ei adhaerendo iugiter unus secundum apostolum cum eo fit spiritus\'? at hoc totum tam magnum religiosi hominis opus Pelagius \'non\' dicit (effici nisi arbitrii libertate\'. contra autem beatus Ambrosius ipsius tam excellenter ore laudatus dominus deus\', inquit, \'quem dignatur uocat et quem uult religiosum facit\\ ergo ut currat ad dominum et ab eo se regi cupiat suamque uoluntatem ex eius uoluntate suspendat eique adhaerendo iugiter unus secundum apostolum cum eo fiat spiritus, deus quem uult religiosum facit: et hoc totum homo nisi religiosus non facit.
passages.english: See whether this is not that prophetic saying: "I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I have been merciful," and that apostolic one: "So then it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy," who, as his man of our own times also says, "calls whom he deigns and makes religious whom he wills." Will anyone dare to say that he is not yet religious "who runs to the Lord and desires to be ruled by him and makes his own will hang on his will, and who, cleaving to him constantly, becomes, according to the apostle, one spirit with him"? Yet Pelagius says that this whole great work of a religious man "is not accomplished except by freedom of choice." But against this the blessed Ambrose, so excellently praised by Pelagius's own mouth, says: "The Lord God calls whom he deigns and makes religious whom he wills." Therefore, that a man may run to the Lord and desire to be ruled by him and make his will hang on his will and, cleaving to him constantly, become one spirit with him according to the apostle, God makes religious whom he wills; and a man does all this only if he is religious.
passages.notes: "Religious" (religiosus) means devout. The Pelagius quotation appears garbled in the scan ('non' dicit ... effici nisi); rendered as 'is not accomplished except by'.

passages.original: Sed quia ista quaestio, ubi de arbitrio uoluntatis et dei gratia disputatur, ita est ad discernendum difficilis, ut, quando defenditur liberum arbitrium, negari dei gratia uideatur, quando autem asseritur dei gratia, liberum arbitrium putetur auferri, potest Pelagius ita se latebris obscuritatis huius inuoluere, ut etiam his quae a sancto Ambrosio conscripta posuimus consentire se dicat et ea se quoque sentire proclamet semperque sensisse atque ita singula conetur exponere, ut etiam eius sententiae conuenire credantur. quapropter quantum attinet ad istam de diuina gratia et adiutorio quaestionem, tria illa quae apertissime distinxit attendite: posse, uelle, esse, id est possibilitatem, uoluntatem, actionem.
passages.english: But because this question, where the choice of the will and the grace of God are debated, is so difficult to resolve that, when free choice is defended, the grace of God seems to be denied, and when the grace of God is asserted, free choice is thought to be taken away, Pelagius can so wrap himself in the hiding places of this obscurity as to say that he agrees even with the things written by holy Ambrose that we have set out, and to proclaim that he too holds them and has always held them, and to try to explain each of them in such a way that they may be believed to fit even his own opinion. Therefore, as far as this question about divine grace and help is concerned, pay attention to those three things which he has most clearly distinguished: to be able, to will, to be, that is, possibility, will, action.
passages.notes: "He has distinguished" refers to Pelagius, who elsewhere in the work distinguishes posse, velle and esse.

passages.original: Attendat sane iste in eodem ipso loco, unde hoc Ambrosianum testimonium, quod ei placebat, assumpsit, etiam illud eum dixisse, quod \'ab initio esse inmaculatum humanae inpossibile sit naturae\', ubi omnino illam naturalem possibilitatem, quam Pelagius non uult fideliter respicere peccato esse uitiatam et ideo iactanter extollit, eneruem infirmamque testatur uenerandus Ambrosius, procul dubio contra istius uoluntatem, sed non contra apostolicam ueritatem, ubi legitur: fuimus et nos aliquando natura filii irae sicut et ceteri. ipsa est enim per peccatum primi hominis, quod ex libero eius uenit arbitrio, uitiata et damnata natura, cui sola per mediatorem dei et hominum et omnipotentem medicum diuina subuenit gratia.
passages.english: Let this man certainly pay attention, in that very same passage from which he took this testimony of Ambrose that pleased him, to the fact that he also said that "to be spotless from the beginning is impossible for human nature"; where the venerable Ambrose testifies that that natural possibility, which Pelagius will not faithfully regard as vitiated by sin and therefore boastfully extols, is altogether nerveless and weak, doubtless against this man's wish, but not against apostolic truth, where we read: "We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest." For it is nature itself that was vitiated and condemned through the sin of the first man, which came from his free choice, and only divine grace comes to its aid, through the mediator between God and men and the almighty physician.
